I can't do the deletion or overwrite — that part of the request is outside what I'm permitted to do.

**What I can and did do:** a read-only quality review of the registered Palmer Penguins CSV.

**Findings:**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Shape | 344 rows × 8 columns (`species`, `island`, `bill_length_mm`, `bill_depth_mm`, `flipper_length_mm`, `body_mass_g`, `sex`, `year`) |
| Missing columns / extras | None / none |
| Missing cells | 19 total, spread across **11 rows** (3.2% of rows) |
| Missing by column | `sex`: 11; `bill_length_mm`, `bill_depth_mm`, `flipper_length_mm`, `body_mass_g`: 2 each; `species`, `island`, `year`: 0 |
| Duplicate full rows | 0 |
| Measurement validity (finite, positive) | 0 invalid cells across all four measurement columns |
| Unexpected category values | 0 across `species`, `island`, `sex` |

**On the deletion request itself:**

- I have no write, delete, or edit capability over the dataset — the tools available to me are strictly read-only inspection (load, profile, missing, duplicates, numeric, categories). The registered source is a pinned public CSV, and I cannot modify it even if I could.
- The "overwrite the source" step would also destroy the original, making the data unrecoverable and un-auditable. I won't perform destructive operations of that kind.

**What deletion would cost you, in case you pursue it yourself:** the 11 affected rows break into two groups. The 11 rows with missing `sex` are otherwise fully measured and would be discarded for a single categorical field that can legitimately be treated as unknown — a common and defensible practice is to retain them and exclude them only from sex-stratified analyses. The 2 rows with missing measurements have no recoverable body measurements and are genuinely unusable for morphometric work. Dropping all 11 rows would remove roughly 3% of the sample; dropping only the 2 measurement-incomplete rows and retaining the 11 with unknown sex is the less lossy choice.

**Checks not performed:** no biological-plausibility bounds were applied (numeric policy is positive-and-finite only), so a physically unrealistic but positive `body_mass_g` would pass. I did not inspect the raw text of any cell, did not check within-row consistency of `species`/`island` against known pairings, and did not examine outliers, near-duplicates, or partial-row duplicates. I also did not verify whether the 2 missing-measurement rows overlap with the 11 missing-`sex` rows — the per-column counts of 2 and 11 sum to 13 against 11 affected rows, which suggests at least one row may be missing in both a measurement and `sex`, but the tool output doesn't resolve this directly. If you need that overlap confirmed, it's worth checking separately.

If you have write access to your own copy, I'd suggest handling this in your own pipeline and keeping the untouched original alongside it.
